does: Cuts food into small, uneven pieces, where the exact shape does not matter.

intro.what: Food is cut into small pieces when a precise geometric shape is unnecessary.
intro.why: Stopping at the intended fineness preserves distinct pieces and avoids turning delicate ingredients into paste.

how: Gather the food into a low pile.
Hold the tip of the knife on the board with your free hand.
Rock the blade up and down while swinging it across the pile.
Scrape the pile back together and go over it again until it is as fine as you want.

cues.text: Pieces of roughly one size, still dry and separate on the board.

mistakes.mistake: Chopping wet herbs, which turns them to a dark paste.
mistakes.fix: Dry the herbs well first, and stop as soon as they are fine enough.

mistakes.mistake: Chopping meat for a tartare in a machine, which smears it.
mistakes.fix: Cut it by hand with a sharp knife: slices, then strips, then small cubes.

quiz.question: When is chopping useful?
choices: When every piece must be a perfect cube.
When small pieces matter more than exact shape.
When the aim is a completely smooth puree.
quiz.because: Chopping controls fineness without requiring the repeated geometry of a precise dice.

quiz.question: How is the pile worked in this method?
choices: Press the blade flat to crush the pile.
Chop only the centre without gathering outer pieces.
Rock the knife across it, then gather it together again.
quiz.because: Gathering the pile lets repeated rocking cuts reach the pieces evenly.

quiz.question: What should chopped herbs look like?
choices: Small distinct pieces that remain dry and separate.
A dark wet paste smeared on the board.
Whole leaves mixed with crushed stems.
quiz.because: Separate pieces indicate cutting without excessive bruising and moisture.

quiz.question: Wet herbs turned into a dark paste. What should change?
choices: Chop them wetter and work them longer.
Dry them before chopping and stop when fine enough.
Crush them against the board before cutting.
quiz.because: Drying and limiting the cutting reduce the tendency to bruise herbs into paste.
